questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the standard dynamic program for the longest common subsequence of two strings of lengths m and n?
questions.explanation: The DP fills an (m+1) by (n+1) table, each cell in constant time from its neighbours. Space can be reduced to O(min(m, n)) since each row depends only on the previous one.

questions.prompt: The edit distance (Levenshtein) between two strings of lengths m and n is computed in:
questions.explanation: Each cell dp[i][j] combines the insert, delete and replace options from adjacent cells in constant time, filling an m by n grid. It measures the minimum single-character edits to transform one string into the other.

questions.prompt: A grid path-counting DP (moving only right or down from top-left to bottom-right of an m by n grid) runs in:
questions.explanation: Each cell's path count is the sum of the cell above and the cell to the left, filling the grid once. The exponential naive recursion recomputes the same cells repeatedly.

questions.prompt: Matrix chain multiplication, which finds the optimal parenthesisation to minimise scalar multiplications, has a DP complexity of:
questions.explanation: The interval DP considers every subchain and every split point within it, giving O(n^3). It decides the multiplication order, not the products themselves.

questions.prompt: The longest palindromic subsequence of a string of length n is found by DP in:
questions.explanation: The interval DP over start and end indices fills an n by n table. It is equivalent to the longest common subsequence of the string and its reverse.

questions.prompt: In interval dynamic programming, subproblems are typically indexed by:

options.text: A pair of endpoints defining a subrange

questions.explanation: Problems like matrix chain and palindrome DP define dp[i][j] over the subrange from i to j, combining results across a split point k inside it. This two-endpoint indexing is the hallmark of interval DP.

questions.prompt: The best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock problem with at most k transactions is solved by a DP in:
questions.explanation: The state tracks the day and the number of transactions used, giving n x k states each updated in constant time. When k is unbounded the problem collapses to a simple greedy scan.

questions.prompt: Why is the DP for LCS often reduced to O(min(m, n)) space?

options.text: The strings are always equal length
Each row of the table depends only on the immediately preceding row
The answer is always the shorter string

questions.explanation: Since dp[i][j] uses only row i-1, two rows (or one, updated carefully) suffice, so only the shorter dimension need be kept. Reconstructing the actual subsequence, however, needs the full table or a divide-and-conquer trick.

questions.prompt: Bitmask dynamic programming, as used for the travelling salesman problem, has what complexity for n cities?
questions.explanation: The state is a subset of visited cities (2^n of them) paired with the current city (n), and each transition tries n next cities, giving O(n^2 x 2^n). This beats the O(n!) brute force for moderate n.

questions.prompt: In a DP on a tree, subproblems are usually defined:

options.text: Per subtree, combining children's results at each node

questions.explanation: Tree DP computes an answer for each node from the answers of its children in a post-order traversal, so each subtree is solved once. Problems like maximum independent set on a tree use exactly this structure.
